subject: pmax
stance: PMax isn't a campaign, it's a deal — and when it 'works amazing', check how much of the win was just your own brand name.

subject: google-ads
stance: Negatives aren't cleanup, they're sculpting. Campaign or ad-group level only — shared lists are negatives nobody remembers, blocking queries nobody checks.

subject: merchant-centre
stance: Everyone blames the campaign when Shopping underperforms, but the feed IS the campaign. One hour in the feed beats ten in campaign settings.

subject: tracking
stance: If you didn't SEE a test conversion land in the platform, your tracking is not live — it's a hope. Smart Bidding on broken tracking is a slot machine.

subject: file-management
stance: Devs show off tools marketers can't use; marketers share prompts that don't compound. Give the AI memory — per-client state, decisions, lessons — or start from zero every day.

subject: vibe-coding
stance: You don't need to learn to code — you need to learn to specify and verify. Never let the AI say 'done' without proof.

subject: content
stance: Logging mistakes feels like admitting failure, so nobody does it — which is exactly why doing it is an advantage. The scars become the curriculum.

subject: tracking
stance: This is the opener and the whole positioning: digital marketing is sold as trackable, and the honest truth is you can't track shit as cleanly as they tell you. Nobody's giving real feedback from real accounts. I run them every day — I'll just show you what I'm actually seeing and testing.

subject: google-ads
stance: Every 'one weird trick' video is lying by omission. Real marketing is holding ten factors in your head and making a judgment call. That's the skill nobody teaches — so I'm going to show the considerations behind real decisions, not just the decisions.

subject: pmax
stance: PMax doesn't fail loudly — it fails profitably-looking. The report says it's your best campaign while it quietly eats your brand traffic and optimises to a broken signal. Here's what I actually check before I believe a PMax number.

subject: ai-max
stance: AI Max isn't set-and-forget, it's set-and-watch-it-spend. I've watched it sail past CPC ceilings and match to searches no human would approve. The issue isn't the product — it's people turning on maximum automation with minimum supervision.

subject: google-ads
stance: Search campaigns fail in boring ways, not exotic ones. The structure doesn't match how people actually search, the match types are set to 'whatever Google suggested', and the ad says something the searcher never asked about. Boring problems, massive money.

subject: google-ads
stance: SKAG as default, STAG as the exception — that's my actual stance from actual accounts, and it's the opposite of what every recycled article says. The point isn't the acronym, it's control: knowing exactly which search triggered which ad. Loosen only when the data says you can.

subject: tracking
stance: Most reports exist to look like work, not to drive a decision. If a report doesn't define what a conversion IS, show what it cost, and say what changes next month, it's decoration. I'd rather send three numbers and one decision than twelve pages of charts.

subject: tracking
stance: The gap isn't access to data, it's knowing which question to ask it. Nobody teaches you to start from a business question and work backwards to the report. So people quote whatever number the default screen shows — which is usually the least useful one in the building.

subject: google-ads
stance: Volume is the least interesting column in the sheet. Intent is the game: what is this person actually trying to do, and are they trying to BUY? A hundred searches with buying intent beats ten thousand lookers every single month.

subject: tracking
stance: Your attribution is only as honest as your parameters, and almost nobody ever looks at them. One broken tracking template and a whole channel reports as 'direct'. It's the least sexy audit in marketing and one of the highest-value ones.

subject: microsoft-ads
stance: Microsoft Ads isn't a Google replacement, it's the cheap second serving of the same demand. Import your proven Google campaigns, fix the quirks the import gets wrong, and you've bought the same searches at a discount. Most advertisers never bother — which is exactly why it works.

subject: feeds
stance: Every attribute in your feed is a separate dial, not a duplicate: the title targets searches, product type structures your campaigns, the Google category tells the algorithm what the thing IS, brand and MPN match you to demand. Treat them as one blob and every dial is set to 'default'.

subject: visibility
stance: Invisibility isn't one problem, it's a stack of small neglects: no content, no profiles, no reviews, a site that doesn't say what you do. The good news is each one is fixable. The bad news is you can't fix what you've never audited — most owners have no idea they're invisible.

subject: content
stance: Rankings aren't withheld from you, they're unearned. Every question your customers ask is a page you haven't written. You don't need clever SEO — you need to actually say things. Volume of genuine answers beats optimisation of nothing.

subject: pr
stance: PR isn't a luxury add-on to SEO, it's half the algorithm. Links and mentions are votes, and most small businesses have never earned a single one on purpose. You don't need a PR agency — you need to give people one reason to reference you.

subject: site-structure
stance: Structure is the silent killer: Google discovers and values pages through your site's own links, and most sites are built around how the business thinks, not how customers search. If a page matters, the structure has to SAY it matters.

subject: content
stance: This kills rankings AND conversions in one shot: if your pages don't say plainly what you do, Google can't match you to searches and visitors can't match you to their problem. The fix isn't copywriting tricks — it's having the guts to be plain.

subject: visibility
stance: Social proof isn't vanity, it's the tiebreaker in every comparison a customer makes — and reviews feed local rankings on top of it. The brutal part: your happiest customers would leave reviews, you just never built the two-minute habit of asking.

subject: page-titles
stance: A page title is your ranking signal AND your ad copy in the results, and most sites burn it on their own name. One line, two jobs, massive leverage — and it's also fragile: lose your titles in a site change and your rankings walk out the door with them.

subject: local-profiles
stance: These profiles are free, they rank in searches your website never will, and they're often the FIRST thing a customer sees about you. An hour of setup across the big three beats months of SEO for local intent — and almost nobody does all three.

subject: search-console
stance: People pay for rank trackers while the search engines hand them the real data for nothing. These two tools are your organic ground truth — and the first place I look on any new site, because they tell you what Google and Microsoft actually think of you, not what a third-party tool estimates.

subject: visibility
stance: SEO now means being the answer in three places: Google, Microsoft, and the AI layer on top of both. The inputs barely changed — clear content, real authority, being referenced — but the stakes did: AI gives ONE answer, not ten blue links. Second place used to get clicks. Now it gets nothing.

subject: targeting
stance: This one's personal: we were the same. We used to post shit about being 'SEO experts' and wonder why nobody cared. The audience was never missing — the way we talked to them was. Now I can sit down and show you what I've actually done to get rankings higher, and THAT people watch.

subject: targeting
stance: Targeting isn't a settings panel, it's knowing a real person: what they're worried about, what they'd type, what makes them stop scrolling. Get the person right and the platform settings almost write themselves. Get it wrong and no amount of audience stacking saves you.

subject: meta
stance: You don't have a content problem, you have a volume and hooks problem. One idea should become ten pieces with ten different front doors. The first three seconds decide everything, and most brands spend their effort on the part of the video nobody reaches.

subject: meta
stance: Organic content is the landing page of your paid social — people check who you ARE before they buy. A feed with no life undoes the ad that brought them. You don't need viral, you need alive: real work, real faces, real answers, consistently.

subject: advantage-plus
stance: Advantage+ amplifies whatever signal you feed it. Strong pixel, clean conversions, broad appeal product? Let it run. Thin data, niche audience, or a conversion event that doesn't mean money? You just gave the wheel to a driver reading the wrong map. The tool isn't good or bad — your signal is.

subject: parameters
stance: Social attribution is already the hardest in marketing — iOS took a bite, platforms over-claim, journeys cross devices. Walking in with broken plumbing on top of that means every conclusion you draw is fiction. Fix the pixel, define the events, tag the links — THEN have opinions.

subject: meta
stance: I use AI all day — for systems, research, drafts, speed. But the moment the POINT of the content is you, outsourcing the voice kills the asset. AI should multiply your take, not replace it. If the idea isn't yours, the volume just scales the emptiness.

subject: skills
stance: The gap between AI dabblers and AI operators isn't prompting talent, it's infrastructure: skills that package your way of doing a task, plugins that connect your actual tools, instructions that persist. Raw chat is a demo. The setup is the product.

subject: workflows
stance: This is the biggest gap I see, honestly. A tool you visit changes nothing; a workflow you rebuilt around AI changes the economics of your whole job. The question isn't 'what can AI do' — it's 'which of my repeating processes should it be welded into first?'

subject: jobs
stance: A job that runs isn't a job that works. Set-and-forget is a lie — it's set-and-VERIFY, forever. The unglamorous truth of automation is that every little job needs a heartbeat, a failure alert, and someone who notices when it's quietly wrong. That's the price, and it's worth paying — knowingly.

subject: vibe-coding
stance: You don't have to become a developer, but you can't skip verification. My rule set: never trust 'done' without proof, read back what actually changed, test on something that can't hurt you first. The AI writes; you verify. Lose that second half and you're not building, you're gambling.

subject: apis
stance: An API is just a waiter: you ask in the right format, it brings the dish. With AI writing the requests, 'I'm not technical' stopped being a reason years ago. And the flip side matters too — some tools have NO API, and that should now be a real factor in what you buy.

subject: retrieval
stance: The boring stuff IS the system. My AI setup works because of decisions nobody makes videos about: one place per kind of file, retrieval that narrows in stages instead of dumping everything, caching so expensive work never runs twice, dedup so the truth exists once. Get the plumbing right and the magic gets reliable.

subject: skills
stance: You don't need to track AI news — you need someone to translate it. My filter is one question: does this feature remove a human step from a real marketing workflow? Bots talking to bots sounds like sci-fi until you realise it means your reporting agent can brief your writing agent. That's an employee chain, not a headline.

subject: workflows
stance: I'm not the AI expert and I'm not trying to be — I'm the marketer who wired it into a real agency and kept what worked. This is the honest tour: where it saves hours, where it needs babysitting, and where we pulled it out because humans were just better.

subject: vibe-coding
stance: Every piece of jargon is a simple idea wearing a bouncer's jacket. A webhook is 'call me when something happens'. A repo is 'a folder with a memory'. I learned this stack as a marketer, from zero — so I'll translate it the way I wish someone had for me, one term at a time.
